messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ahmed, a 30-year-old Middle Eastern man, recently divorced and working as a tax inspector in Los Angeles, has been struggling with profound distress following a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. The event itself was seared into his memory: he had been driving home from work when another car, likely impaired by alcohol, veered into his lane and collided head-on with his vehicle. Ahmed remembers the smell of burning rubber and fuel, the screech of metal grinding against metal, and the overwhelming scent of alcohol that permeated the air. The impact was so severe that it left him trapped inside his car for nearly an hour before he could be extricated by emergency personnel. Since then, Ahmed has been on a downward spiral, unable to shake off the haunting images and visceral reactions. Any sight or smell reminiscent of the crash triggers intense anxiety and panic. The sound of screeching tires or the alcohol aroma wafting from nearby bars are enough to send him into a tailspin. His response to these triggers is to escape into his phone, playing games or browsing the internet for hours on end to avoid confronting his thoughts and emotions. Ahmed had come to believe that he could not rely on himself anymore; the trauma had left him feeling incapable of doing the things that once defined him as competent and strong. This sense of helplessness has further exacerbated his coping mechanisms. He spends long hours on his phone, avoiding social interactions and even driving altogether. His hypervigilance is constant: he is superalert and jumps at unexpected or loud sounds, which only reinforces his belief that he cannot trust himself to navigate the world safely. The fear of encountering another triggering situation has led him to avoid driving entirely, severely limiting his ability to perform essential tasks required for his job as a tax inspector. Ahmed’s undereating is also a manifestation of this coping strategy; he often skips meals or restricts his food intake, feeling that controlling something in his life gives him a semblance of order. However, this only deepens the cycle of negative appraisals and maladaptive behaviors. His belief that he will never feel normal emotions again leads him to further isolate himself from others, which makes it harder for him to seek support or find healthy ways to cope. The interplay between his triggers and threats is a self-reinforcing loop. Every time Ahmed encounters a car similar to the one involved in the crash or smells alcohol, he becomes hyperalert, certain that danger lurks around every corner. This hypervigilance only heightens his anxiety and reinforces the idea that he cannot trust himself to handle these situations. As a result, he retreats even further into avoidance behaviors like playing games on his phone for hours. Ahmed’s work as a tax inspector has become increasingly difficult due to his inability to drive to inspections or meetings outside of his immediate office location. His colleagues have noticed his absence and the quality of his work has suffered, leading to tension with supervisors who are growing concerned about his performance. The realization that he is no longer capable of fulfilling his professional responsibilities further erodes his self-esteem and reinforces his negative appraisals. What finally brought Ahmed to seek help was a combination of increasing isolation, worsening anxiety attacks at the mere thought of leaving his house, and the fear that he would lose his job if things didn’t improve. He is most afraid of never being able to return to his former self or feeling like a burden on others due to his struggles. At the same time, Ahmed hopes for a way to regain some sense of control over his life and find healthier coping mechanisms to deal with his trauma. Through the lens of Ehlers & Clark’s (2000) cognitive model, it is evident that Ahmed's core negative appraisals are driving both his maladaptive strategies and heightened threat monitoring. His triggers, while potent, are also part of a broader cycle where each component fuels the other in a relentless feedback loop. Seeking help represents a critical step for Ahmed to break this cycle and regain some semblance of control over his life.
